transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-09-15
Time: 14:00 PT
Duration: ~58 minutes
Attendees: Emily Chen (Redwood AE), Priya Raman (Redwood SE), Jordan Lee (Nimbus SRE), Maya Thompson (Nimbus CTO), Liam Park (Nimbus ML Eng)
Shared artifacts: link to Redwood KV-cache deep dive deck (redwood.link/kv-deck), benchmark spreadsheet (drive.google.com/spreadsheet/kv-bench), sample logs uploaded to Nimbus shared drive (note)

Summary (auto):
Customer experiencing sporadic KV cache evictions on Dedicated cluster causing latency spikes for long-context sessions. They see paging behavior, and prefix reuse patterns that sometimes prevent reuse. Wants architecture explanation, reproduction guidance, and next steps to debug in prod.

Topics: KV cache architecture, eviction policies, paging, long-context handling, prefix reuse heuristics, batching interaction, quantization impact, VPC/on-prem considerations

Transcript:
[00:00] Emily (AE): Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Priya and I will do a deep dive on the KV cache behavior you saw. Jordan, Maya, Liam, thanks for making time. Do you want to do a quick framing of what you're seeing?
[00:18] Jordan (SRE): Yeah thanks. So we run a dedicated Redwood cluster in our VPC. Over the last 2 weeks we've had intermittent latency spikes where requests that normally come back in ~80ms go to 800-1,200ms. It correlates with long documents — 16k to 32k tokens — and we see a boom in memory usage followed by a bunch of eviction warnings.
[00:36] Maya (CTO): The core problem for us is a subset of customer queries that reuse a long prefix. We expect prefix reuse to be cached heavily, but sometimes the cache isn't reused and we get paging or evictions which kills tail latency.
[00:50] Priya (SE): Got it. Thanks. A couple quick questions: which model family are you running, and are you using KV cache pinning or any custom cache policy?
[00:58] Liam (ML Eng): We're on an open-variant gptx-34b-ql-ggml-ish — sorry, internal shorthand — quantized to int8. We don't pin prefixes. We use Redwood Dedicated with default cache settings; autoscaling is enabled but we hit memory pressure before scale completes.
[01:18] Priya: No worries on the model name, we see that a lot in transcriptions. Int8 quantization matters because it changes activation sizes and how the runtime lays out KV pages. Can you share the eviction logs?
[01:28] Jordan: Uploaded a trimmed set. The pattern is: long chat session, repeated reuse of a conversation prefix across multiple independent requests, then a flush of older KV segments and immediate paging. We also saw a flurry of small batches while a large batch was forming.
[01:45] Priya: Awesome, that matches a few hypotheses. Architecture primer quick: in our runtime the KV cache is sharded per-GPU with a fast on-GPU region and a fallback paged region that may live in host memory or be swapped. We have eviction policies tuned for LRU with heuristics around prefix hotness and sequence-length-aware weights. However, when many concurrent sessions reuse slightly different prefixes (think same start but injected tokens) the heuristic can fail to coalesce and you get duplicate KV entries.
[02:16] Emily: I'll interrupt — can you explain 'duplicate KV entries' for the team?
[02:20] Priya: Sure. If the prefix differs by token offsets or metadata (like different system messages), the runtime treats them as distinct cache entries. So if Users A and B have a 4-token difference at the end of the prefix, that can prevent reuse and cause higher total KV size.
[02:34] Maya: That rings bells — we do templating where we append small user-specific tokens. Might be the culprit.
[02:40] Priya: Another factor is batching. Continuous batching aggregates requests and can increase peak memory because multiple sessions' KV caches are resident until batch completion. If autoscale lags, memory peaks and the eviction logic prioritizes keeping the most recently accessed segments, which sometimes evicts a hot prefix that was momentarily idle due to scheduling.
[03:05] Jordan: We noticed evictions align with spikes in small-batch traffic; typically background jobs + interactive requests.
[03:12] Priya: Exactly. Two concrete behaviors to watch: 1) prefix fragmentation (small variations causing duplicate entries) and 2) batch-induced retention that creates transient memory hotspots.
[03:26] Liam: Any guidance on reproducing this in staging?
[03:29] Priya: Yes — we'll provide a reproducer script. At a high level: spawn N concurrent sessions with controlled slight variations in the last ~5 tokens of a shared prefix; set inter-arrival times to produce small batches and occasional large batches; measure per-GPU KV size, eviction counts, and host paging metrics. We'll also share PromQL queries to extract eviction_rate, kv_cache_size_bytes, and host_swap_in/out.
[03:56] Emily: We'll attach a checklist for getting those metrics from your Dedicated cluster.
[04:00] Jordan: Thanks. A question — you mentioned heuristics favor prefix hotness. How does that interact with long-context? We have sessions where the context grows beyond 20k and the model still needs the earliest tokens because users do long-document Q&A.
[04:14] Priya: Good question. For extremely long contexts we rely on two mechanisms: automatic partial eviction with prefix compaction (we keep checkpoints and prune older KV snapshots while preserving token positions), and on-demand paging where older KV segments are paged in from host memory. But both have tradeoffs: compaction may require recomputing attention for holes which increases CPU overhead; paging increases tail latency due to PCIe/host read times on Dedicated hosts.
[04:42] Maya: Is compaction safe for correctness? We can't lose information for long-document QA.
[04:46] Priya: Correctness is preserved — compaction keeps sufficient checkpoints so that on recompute we can reconstruct attention keys. There's a cost in extra compute, but it avoids excessive host swapping which is often worse for tail latency. We can tune checkpoint frequency.
[04:59] Liam: And quantization — you said it affects layout. How much does it change the memory footprint?
[05:04] Priya: Int8 vs fp16 can be roughly 2x difference in activation size; but layout and alignment overhead can change expected page boundaries. In some cases quantized kernels require extra metadata per KV shard, so the effective increase may not be linear. That sometimes causes earlier than expected eviction thresholds.
[05:23] Jordan: We saw odd boundary churn in the logs — pages being moved around even though absolute bytes seemed constant. Could that be alignment overhead?
[05:29] Priya: Yes. Also different kernels reserve padding for vectorized paths. We'll need to look at the kernel/quantization profile from your run.
[05:36] Emily: Let's talk about prefix reuse heuristics — is there a way to coalesce near-identical prefixes on your side?
[05:42] Priya: There are a few levers: 1) client-side canonicalization where you normalize templated tokens so the exact prefix text is identical; 2) Redwood-side fuzzy hashing that can map near-identical prefixes to the same cache key if you opt-in (we can enable a conservative mode for your Dedicated cluster); 3) pinning important prefixes into a protected cache region. Pinning is most deterministic but consumes reserved memory.
[06:08] Maya: What's the memory cost for pinning? We have predictable usage for about 200 hot sessions at peak.
[06:15] Priya: Depends on average token length of each pinned prefix. Rough back-of-envelope: pinned_prefix_memory = average_prefix_tokens * per_token_kv_bytes * number_of_prefixes. We'll help compute this after we see your prefix lengths. Pinning is recommended when you have a small set of very hot prefixes.
[06:30] Jordan: We also run in a VPC with limited host memory per node because of other co-located services. Would pinning risk OOM for other workloads?
[06:38] Priya: It could if you pin lots of prefixes. Another option is to move to a Dedicated SKU with higher memory headroom or enable burst nodes. Also our autoscaler can be tuned to scale earlier (lower threshold) to prevent hitting eviction heuristics.
[06:52] Liam: Any tradeoffs for lowering autoscale threshold? Cost impact?
[06:55] Priya: More headroom means more idle costs; the Optimize toolkit can simulate cost/latency tradeoffs and suggest middle ground. We'll run a cost simulation for your traffic shape.
[07:05] Maya: You mentioned host paging. For on-prem deployments where we don't want host swapping, are there recommended config changes?
[07:12] Priya: For on-prem you typically want to disable host paging and size the host memory to fit peak KV + model footprint. If that's infeasible, enable prefix pinning for critical flows and compaction for the rest. Also ensure NUMA and GPU-affinity are tuned.
[07:28] Jordan: We saw paging slowness correlate with PCIe gen mismatches on one of our node types — older gen vs newer gen. Should we standardize hardware?
[07:36] Priya: Yes heterogenous PCIe bandwidth can create hotspots; we recommend homogenous node profiles for Dedicated pools or a routing policy that avoids sending latency-sensitive flows to older nodes. Our smart routing can do that.
[07:48] Emily: Let's dig into repro steps and metrics. Priya, can you list the exact PromQL and logging keys we should look for?
[07:54] Priya: Sure. High-level metrics: redwood_kv_evictions_total, redwood_kv_pages_fetched_total, redwood_kv_size_bytes, redwood_batch_size_current, container_memory_rss_bytes, host_swap_in_bytes. For logs: look for tags kv.eviction.reason and kv.page.fetch.latency_ms. We'll share exact queries in the checklist.
[08:15] Jordan: Great. We'll run those queries and correlate with user sessions.
[08:19] Liam: A corner case — we use per-request metadata headers that add small differences to prefixes. Any quick win to minimize fragmentation without changing client logic?
[08:27] Priya: You can canonicalize headers server-side before creating KV keys, or we can provide a middleware in the Redwood SDK that strips or normalizes non-essential tokens prior to caching. That's lower friction than changing all clients.
[08:40] Maya: We also need to think about security — if you pin prefixes, are those contents logged or encrypted? We have strict PII rules.
[08:47] Emily: Good point. We'll attach how pinning interacts with KMS and audit logs. Priya, quick note on encryption?
[08:52] Priya: Pinned prefixes live in the same encrypted memory space; on Dedicated we integrate with customer KMS for control plane secrets. KV content at rest isn't stored persistently in most setups but we can enable audit hooks and additional redaction. We'll follow up with a security doc.
[09:08] Jordan: In terms of timeline we need a prioritized list: what's lowest lift / highest impact?
[09:12] Priya: 1) client-side canonicalization (low lift if you can change templates) 2) enable conservative fuzzy-hash coalescing (low-medium lift on Redwood side) 3) prefix pinning for top N hot prefixes (medium lift) 4) adjust autoscale thresholds and consider larger Dedicated instances (medium-high lift) 5) hardware homogenization (high lift).
[09:36] Emily: We're going to send a prioritized runbook and the reproducer.
[09:40] Jordan: Great. A couple of nitty-gritty questions: how does continuous batching interact with KV eviction timing? We saw eviction occur mid-batch which made the request fail and fall back to slower path.
[09:50] Priya: Continuous batching holds KV partitions pinned for the lifetime of a batch. If an eviction is triggered mid-batch, we favor batch completion to preserve throughput and completeness — that can temporarily increase memory, leading to cascading evictions elsewhere. We have a configurable knob to prefer eviction ahead of batch completion if you want more predictable memory footprint at the cost of some batch efficiency.
[10:15] Liam: Is there a metric to detect prefix fragmentation easily?
[10:18] Priya: Yes — compute unique_cache_keys / total_sessions over a sliding window. If that ratio is high (>0.7) it means many unique keys vs sessions indicating fragmentation. We'll provide the exact query.
[10:29] Maya: For our long-context users we sometimes want early pruning but preserve retrievability. You mentioned checkpoint frequency. What's a sane default?
[10:36] Priya: Start with checkpoints every ~2k tokens for 32k contexts. That tends to balance recompute cost vs paging. If recompute latency is tolerable for you, you can increase checkpoint spacing to save memory.
[10:47] Jordan: Ok. We'll try reproducer + canonicalization first. Can you also share the fuzzy-hash toggle?
[10:53] Priya: Yes, we'll flip it in a canary mode on one node pool so we can observe any mis-coalescing. It has safety limits.
[11:02] Emily: Anything else on quantization?
[11:04] Priya: Only that if you upgrade quantization scheme (e.g., grouped-quantization) we can provide kernel profiles to show expected KV footprint changes. We'll sync offline on that.
[11:15] Maya: Last question — any known bugs in the current runtime that could cause spurious evictions?
[11:20] Priya: There's an older issue on eviction accounting in mixed GPU types which we patched in the 2025-08 runtime; but if you're on an earlier build that could explain the churn. Jordan, can you share the runtime version?
[11:29] Jordan: We're on 2025-06-12 build.
[11:32] Priya: That explains it — the fix is in later builds. We'll recommend an upgrade path; we'll provide the release notes and a canary plan.
[11:40] Emily: Ok wrapping — quick recap of agreed next steps so we're aligned.
[11:45] Jordan: Go ahead.
[11:46] Emily: Priya will provide the reproducer, PromQL queries, and fuzzy-hash toggle steps. Priya will also provide pinning cost calc worksheet. Jordan and Liam will run the reproducer in staging, collect eviction traces and upload logs. Emily will send pricing for Dedicated headroom and security docs. We'll schedule follow-up the week of 2025-09-22 to validate results.
[12:06] Maya: That sounds good. Thanks everyone.
[12:10] Liam: Thanks.
[12:12] Emily: I'll also drop the benchmark spreadsheet and the deck in the follow-up email.

End of transcript.

Explicit next steps (restated):
- Redwood to share: reproducer script, PromQL queries, fuzzy-hash conservative mode toggle instructions, pinning cost calc sheet, runtime upgrade notes, security docs and pricing.
- Nimbus to run reproducer in staging, gather logs (kv.eviction.*, kv.page.*), share traces, and confirm if client-side canonicalization is feasible.

Notes on transcription quality: some model names and kernel/quant names transcribed imperfectly. Refer to artifacts for exact logs.

Recommended immediate wins: canonicalize templated tokens, run reproducer, enable conservative fuzzy coalescing in canary, calculate pinning memory for top 200 prefixes.
